titre: Steno, 1669: A Shark's Head Opens the Layers of Time
accroche: In 1666, a shark's head dissected in Florence leads Nicolas Steno to ask how one solid forms inside another solid.
contenu_vulgarise:
In October 1666, two fishermen caught a huge female shark near Livorno. The Grand Duke of Tuscany, Ferdinand II de' Medici, ordered the head sent to Nicolas Steno, a Dane who had settled in Italy that year, first as a professor of anatomy in Padua, then as the grand duke's physician in Florence. Steno dissected the head, examined the rows of teeth, and noticed a troubling resemblance to “glossopetrae,” “tongue stones” found in rock. Pliny had suggested they fell from the sky or from the Moon, and others thought fossils grew naturally inside rocks.

## A Solid Inside Another Solid

If glossopetrae are really shark teeth, one has to explain how an object of animal origin ended up inside solid rock. Steno published his answer in 1669 in Florence, in a text with a modest title: *De solido intra solidum naturaliter contento dissertationis prodromus* (“Preliminary Discourse to a Dissertation on a Solid Naturally Contained Within a Solid”). His reasoning rests on surfaces of contact: when one solid encloses another, the shape of one bears the imprint of the other, and it is easy, he writes about incrustations, to determine which hardened first and which last. In John Garrett Winter's English translation (1916), if the place was concave, the outer layers formed first; if convex, the inner ones.

## Strata as a Chronology

Steno then applies this reasoning to rock layers themselves. He writes that when one of the upper strata was being formed, the lower stratum had already gained the consistency of a solid: the lowest is therefore the oldest. He adds that the upper surface of a layer is parallel to the horizon, and that its lower and lateral surfaces match those of what supports it. According to Wikipedia, the 1669 Prodromus contains four principles of stratigraphy: superposition, original horizontality, lateral continuity, and cross-cutting relationships. Together they turn a pile of rocks into a sequence that can be put in order: bottom before top, horizontal at the origin, lateral continuity up to an obstacle.

## What This Changes

Steno dates no stratum in years: he only gives them a relative order. But that order makes a pile of rocks a story in which each layer has a before and an after, rather than a frozen state. It all starts with a shark's head on the table of a Danish physician, and a question that could have remained an anatomist's curiosity, with no consequence for understanding the Earth.

carte.punch: A shark's head in 1666 leads Steno to state: the lowest stratum is the oldest.
carte.idee: In 1669, Nicolas Steno writes that, in a stack of rocks, the bottom layer had already gained the consistency of a solid when the top one formed. Born from a shark's tooth, this reasoning lets geologists read strata as a relative chronology.

quiz.question: What does Steno write about the lower layer at the time an upper layer is forming?
choix: That it is still fluid and solidifies at the same time as the upper layer
That it had already gained the consistency of a solid, so the lowest is the oldest
That it always forms after the upper layer, by seeping in from above
That it is always thinner than the upper layer, whatever the rock
quiz.explication: Steno writes that when one of the upper strata was being formed, the lower stratum had already gained the consistency of a solid: the lowest is therefore the oldest. The other options do not appear in his reasoning.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where do two fishermen catch the female shark whose head is sent to Steno?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places the catch near Livorno, in October 1666. Padua and Florence are the cities where Steno later teaches and practices medicine, not where the fishing took place.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Pliny suggest about glossopetrae, these “tongue stones”?
choix: That they were petrified shark teeth
That they came from the depths of the ocean, washed up by the waves
That they had been carved by fishermen from Livorno
That they fell from the sky or the Moon
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the text, Pliny thought glossopetrae fell from the sky or the Moon. Steno, by contrast, notices their resemblance to shark teeth, which is a different explanation.
